# ISO 27001 Gap Analysis & 9-Month Certification Roadmap

## Your starting position

You're in better shape than many orgs at this stage. SOC 2 Type II work gives you partial coverage of roughly 30–40% of ISO 27001 Annex A controls, and your existing ITIL practices (change board, incident management) provide ready-made evidence. The biggest gaps are likely the ISMS governance layer (Clauses 4–10), formal risk assessment, asset inventory completeness, and vulnerability management maturity.

---

## Part 1: Prioritized Gap Analysis Checklist

I've organized this by priority tier rather than sequential Annex A numbering, because auditors care most about whether your ISMS is coherent and risk-driven, not whether you tackled controls in numerical order.

### Tier 1 — Foundational (do these first; everything else depends on them)

**ISMS governance framework (Clauses 4–6, 9–10)**

| Gap area | What you likely have | What's missing | Evidence auditors expect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Context of the organization (Clause 4) | Informal understanding | Documented scope statement, interested parties register, internal/external issues | Scope document with clear boundaries (AWS accounts, services, locations, exclusions) |
| Leadership and policy (Clause 5) | Possibly ad hoc security policies | Board-endorsed ISMS policy, defined roles (ISMS owner, risk owner), management commitment | Signed ISMS policy, RACI matrix, board/exec meeting minutes showing security agenda items |
| Risk assessment and treatment (Clause 6.1.2–6.1.3) | SOC 2 risk register (partial) | Formal methodology, consistent criteria for likelihood/impact, risk treatment plan, Statement of Applicability | Risk assessment methodology document, risk register with scored risks, treatment plan linked to Annex A controls, SoA with justifications for every included/excluded control |
| Performance evaluation (Clause 9) | SOC 2 monitoring | ISMS internal audit programme, management review process | Internal audit schedule and reports, management review meeting minutes with defined agenda per Clause 9.3 |
| Continual improvement (Clause 10) | Incident post-mortems | Formal corrective action process, nonconformity tracking | Corrective action log with root cause analysis, evidence of closure |

**Asset management and classification (Annex A 5.9–5.13)**

| Gap area | What you likely have | What's missing | Evidence auditors expect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Information asset inventory | Partial inventory, AWS resource tags | Comprehensive register covering data assets, software, cloud services, people, physical assets | Asset register with owners assigned, classification labels, review dates |
| Information classification | Possibly informal | Classification scheme (e.g., Public / Internal / Confidential / Restricted), handling procedures | Classification policy, labelling evidence in repos and storage, handling matrix |
| Media and asset disposal | Ad hoc | Documented disposal/return procedures | Disposal logs, AWS resource decommissioning records, offboarding checklists |

**Risk assessment and vulnerability management (Annex A 8.8, 5.7, 8.34)**

| Gap area | What you likely have | What's missing | Evidence auditors expect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vulnerability management | Ad hoc scanning | Formal policy with defined scan frequency, SLAs for remediation by severity, coverage of infra and application layers | Policy document, scan reports (e.g., AWS Inspector, Qualys, Snyk), remediation tickets with timestamps showing SLA compliance, exception/risk-acceptance records |
| Threat intelligence (5.7) | Possibly AWS GuardDuty alerts | Documented process for consuming and acting on threat intel | Procedure document, evidence of feed subscriptions, examples of threat intel leading to action |
| Audit logging and monitoring (8.15–8.16) | EDR, some CloudWatch/CloudTrail | Centralized logging with retention policy, defined alert thresholds, review cadence | Log retention configuration, SIEM or log platform dashboards, alert triage records |

### Tier 2 — Strengthen existing controls (leverage your ITIL and SOC 2 work)

**Access control (Annex A 5.15–5.18, 8.2–8.5)**

| Gap area | What you likely have | What's missing | Evidence auditors expect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Access control policy | MFA deployed, likely role-based access | Documented access control policy covering need-to-know, least privilege, segregation of duties | Policy document, evidence of periodic access reviews (quarterly recommended), recertification records |
| Privileged access (8.2) | Likely some AWS IAM controls | Formal privileged access management (PAM) process, break-glass procedures | PAM tool logs or documented procedure, list of privileged accounts with justification, session recording or audit trail |
| Identity provisioning and deprovisioning | HR/IT onboarding process | Automated joiner-mover-leaver process tied to HR system, timely deprovisioning evidence | Onboarding/offboarding checklists with timestamps, access removal within defined SLA (e.g., 24 hours of termination) |

**Change management (Annex A 8.32, 8.25–8.31)**

| Gap area | What you likely have | What's missing | Evidence auditors expect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Change enablement | Change board (ITIL), CI/CD pipelines | Link between change board approvals and deployment evidence, emergency change procedure, rollback criteria | CAB meeting minutes or Jira/ServiceNow tickets showing approval before deployment, CI/CD pipeline logs showing gate checks (tests, security scans, approval steps), emergency change records with post-implementation review |
| Secure development lifecycle (8.25–8.27) | CI/CD with some testing | Documented SDLC security policy, SAST/DAST in pipeline, code review requirements, separation of dev/test/prod | SDLC policy, pipeline configuration showing security scan stages (e.g., Snyk, SonarQube, OWASP ZAP), PR merge rules requiring review, environment separation evidence in AWS accounts or VPCs |
| Configuration management (8.9) | Likely Terraform/IaC | Formal baseline configurations, drift detection | IaC repos with version history, AWS Config rules or similar drift detection, hardening standards (CIS benchmarks) |

**Incident management (Annex A 5.24–5.28)**

| Gap area | What you likely have | What's missing | Evidence auditors expect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Incident response process | ITIL incident management, PagerDuty or similar | Formal information security incident classification (vs. operational incidents), escalation matrix, breach notification procedure, evidence preservation | Incident response plan document, classification matrix, tabletop exercise records, post-incident reports with root cause and corrective actions, breach notification procedure aligned with GDPR/contractual obligations |

### Tier 3 — Fill remaining gaps

**Supplier management (Annex A 5.19–5.22)**

| Gap area | What you likely have | What's missing | Evidence auditors expect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Supplier security | AWS shared responsibility awareness, possibly some vendor questionnaires for SOC 2 | Supplier register with risk ratings, security clauses in contracts, periodic reassessment | Supplier register, contract clauses or DPAs, evidence of annual review (e.g., requesting SOC 2 reports from critical vendors), AWS shared responsibility documentation |

**People security (Annex A 6.1–6.8)**

| Gap area | What you likely have | What's missing | Evidence auditors expect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Background screening (6.1) | Possibly for some roles | Policy covering all roles proportionate to risk | Screening policy, evidence of checks completed (redacted records) |
| Awareness and training (6.3) | Possibly phishing simulations | Formal security awareness programme with annual training, role-based training for developers and admins | Training platform records showing completion rates, training content, phishing simulation results with trend data |
| Disciplinary process (6.4) | HR policy | Link between security violations and disciplinary procedures | Policy cross-reference, ideally in acceptable use policy |

**Business continuity and backup (Annex A 5.29–5.30, 8.13–8.14)**

| Gap area | What you likely have | What's missing | Evidence auditors expect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Backup (8.13) | AWS snapshots, RDS backups | Documented backup policy with RTOs/RPOs, tested restore procedures | Backup policy, backup configuration evidence, restore test records (at least annual) |
| ICT readiness for business continuity (5.30) | AWS multi-AZ or similar | Documented BCP/DR plan, tested failover | BCP/DR plan, test results, lessons learned |
| Redundancy (8.14) | AWS infrastructure redundancy | Documentation linking redundancy design to availability requirements | Architecture diagrams, availability SLAs, failover evidence |

**Physical and environmental (Annex A 7.1–7.14)**

For a SaaS company on AWS, most physical controls are inherited from AWS (reference their SOC 2 report and ISO 27001 certificate). You still need to cover your own offices: visitor logs, clean desk, physical access controls for any on-premises equipment.

---

## Part 2: 9-Month Certification Roadmap

### Months 1–2: Establish the ISMS and assess risk

**Governance setup**: Draft and get executive sign-off on the ISMS policy, scope document, and roles/responsibilities. Appoint an ISMS manager or owner. Set up an information security steering committee (can be monthly, 30 minutes, with CTO/CISO/VP Eng/Head of IT).

**Risk assessment**: Choose and document a methodology (e.g., ISO 27005-aligned, qualitative 5×5 matrix). Identify information assets by working through your AWS accounts, data stores, SaaS tools, and repositories. Score risks and produce a treatment plan. Draft the Statement of Applicability — this is the single most important document for your audit.

**Quick wins**: Formalize your existing ITIL incident and change processes as ISO 27001 evidence. Map SOC 2 controls to Annex A — your SOC 2 auditor may have a mapping or you can use the AICPA-to-ISO mapping as a starting point.

**DevOps evidence tip**: Export your Jira/ServiceNow change tickets, CI/CD pipeline configurations, and PagerDuty incident timelines now. These become Annex A evidence with minimal reformatting.

**Deliverables**: ISMS scope, ISMS policy, risk assessment methodology, asset register (v1), risk register, treatment plan, Statement of Applicability (draft).

### Months 3–4: Build core policies and close Tier 1 gaps

**Documentation sprint**: Write or formalize the core policy set. At minimum you need policies covering access control, acceptable use, classification, cryptography, backup, vulnerability management, supplier security, secure development, and incident response. Keep them concise — auditors prefer short, enforceable policies over 50-page documents nobody reads.

**Vulnerability management programme**: Deploy or configure automated scanning across infrastructure (AWS Inspector, Qualys, Nessus) and application code (Snyk, Dependabot, SonarQube). Define remediation SLAs (e.g., Critical: 72 hours, High: 7 days, Medium: 30 days, Low: 90 days). Integrate scan results into your ticketing system so you have timestamped evidence of remediation.

**Asset inventory completion**: Use AWS resource tagging, a CMDB, or even a well-maintained spreadsheet. Every asset needs an owner and a classification label.

**Security awareness**: Launch a formal programme. Platforms like KnowBe4 or Proofpoint give you completion dashboards auditors love.

**Deliverables**: Policy library (10–15 policies), vulnerability management procedure with SLAs, complete asset register, awareness training launched.

### Months 5–6: Operationalize controls and generate evidence

**Access reviews**: Run your first formal access recertification across critical systems (AWS IAM, source code repos, production databases, SaaS admin consoles). Document results and remediation of any excess access.

**Supplier register**: Build a register of all third parties with access to your data or systems. Rate them by risk. Collect SOC 2 or ISO 27001 certificates from critical vendors. Ensure contracts contain appropriate security clauses.

**Secure SDLC hardening**: Ensure CI/CD pipelines have mandatory security scan stages that block deployment on critical findings. Document branch protection rules, PR review requirements, and environment separation. Auditors will want to see a pipeline run showing a security gate in action.

**Backup and DR testing**: Run and document a restore test and, if possible, a failover test. Record RTOs achieved versus targets.

**Logging and monitoring**: Ensure CloudTrail, CloudWatch, and your EDR feed into a centralized platform with defined retention (12 months is a common auditor expectation). Document alert rules and triage procedures.

**Deliverables**: Access review records, supplier register, SDLC security evidence, backup/DR test results, logging architecture documentation.

### Months 7–8: Internal audit, management review, and remediation

**Internal audit**: Conduct a full internal audit against Clauses 4–10 and all applicable Annex A controls. Use an independent auditor if possible (external consultant, or at least someone not responsible for the controls being audited). Document findings as nonconformities or observations.

**Management review**: Hold a formal management review meeting covering the agenda items required by Clause 9.3: audit results, risk treatment status, interested party feedback, improvement opportunities. Produce minutes and action items.

**Remediation**: Close nonconformities from the internal audit. Each one needs root cause analysis, corrective action, and evidence of closure. This corrective action cycle is itself evidence that your ISMS works.

**Mock audit (optional but recommended)**: Engage your chosen certification body or an independent consultant for a pre-assessment. This surfaces issues before the real audit.

**Deliverables**: Internal audit report, management review minutes, corrective action log, remediation evidence.

### Month 9: Stage 1 and Stage 2 audits

**Stage 1 (documentation review)**: The certification body reviews your ISMS documentation, SoA, risk assessment, and policies. This is typically a 1–2 day remote or on-site review. They confirm you're ready for Stage 2 and flag any areas of concern. For a 250-person SaaS company, expect roughly 2–3 auditor-days.

**Gap between Stage 1 and Stage 2**: Typically 4–8 weeks. Use this time to address any Stage 1 findings.

**Stage 2 (implementation audit)**: The auditor verifies that controls are implemented and operating effectively. They interview staff, review evidence, and sample records. For your org size, expect roughly 8–12 auditor-days. They will sample change tickets, incident records, access reviews, vulnerability scans, training records, and risk treatment evidence.

**Deliverables**: Stage 1 report clearance, Stage 2 audit passed, certificate issued (typically 4–6 weeks after Stage 2).

---

## Controls to tackle first (priority order and reasoning)

The sequence matters because auditors evaluate your ISMS as a system, not a checklist. The first three items create the structure that makes everything else coherent.

1. **Risk assessment and SoA** — every control decision must trace back to a risk. Without this, nothing else has justification.
2. **ISMS governance documents** — scope, policy, roles. These take days to write but are hard prerequisites for audit.
3. **Asset inventory** — you can't protect what you don't know about, and your risk assessment is hollow without it.
4. **Vulnerability management** — your biggest operational gap. Moving from ad hoc to SLA-driven scanning gives you high-value evidence quickly.
5. **Access control formalization** — you have MFA, so you're ahead. Add periodic reviews and privileged access documentation.
6. **Change and SDLC security** — your DevOps pipeline is an asset here. Add security gates and document what you already do.
7. **Incident response formalization** — extend your ITIL process to cover security-specific classification and breach notification.
8. **Supplier management** — often overlooked and time-consuming because it depends on third parties responding.
9. **Training and awareness** — easy to implement, slow to generate trend data, so start early.
10. **Internal audit and management review** — these prove the ISMS is a living system, not shelfware.

---

## Finishing the cut-off section: What specific evidence auditors sample most heavily

Auditors at Stage 2 will typically ask for live demonstrations and samples across these areas, roughly in order of how much time they spend on each.

**Risk assessment and treatment trail.** They will pick a risk from your register and trace it end to end: from identification, through scoring, to the treatment decision, to the specific Annex A control(s) it maps to in the SoA, to evidence that the control is operating. If this chain breaks at any point, it is a major nonconformity. They may do this three to five times with different risks.

**Change and deployment records.** They will ask you to pull up recent change tickets (often five to ten samples) and show the approval, testing evidence, security scan results, and deployment log. For a DevOps shop, expect them to ask you to walk through a CI/CD pipeline run on screen, showing gate checks, test results, and who approved the merge/deploy.

**Incident records.** They will sample two to four incidents and check for classification, escalation, root cause analysis, corrective actions, and evidence that lessons learned fed back into the ISMS. If you had a security incident, they will examine it in detail. If you had none, they will probe how you would know — which leads to your monitoring and detection evidence.

**Access reviews.** They want to see a completed recertification cycle: who reviewed, what access was found, what was revoked, and when. They will also sample joiner and leaver records to check provisioning and deprovisioning timeliness.

**Vulnerability scan reports and remediation.** They will pull scan reports, pick critical or high findings, and check your ticketing system for evidence that remediation met your SLA. Exceptions or risk acceptances need to be formally documented and approved — ad hoc "we decided to leave it" is a finding.

**Training completion records.** They want dashboards or reports showing completion rates, ideally above 95%, and evidence that new joiners are trained within a defined window.

**Supplier due diligence.** They will pick two to three critical suppliers and ask for the contract security clauses, the last assessment or SOC 2 report you collected, and evidence of periodic review.

**Management review minutes.** They will read these carefully. The minutes must show that the agenda covered the items in Clause 9.3 (risk status, audit results, interested party feedback, opportunities for improvement) and that actions were assigned and tracked.

**Internal audit report.** They will check scope coverage, auditor independence, findings, and corrective actions. If your internal audit found zero nonconformities, they will be skeptical — a mature ISMS always finds something to improve.

**Corrective action records.** For every nonconformity from internal audit or previous external audits, they want root cause analysis, the corrective action taken, evidence of implementation, and evidence of effectiveness verification.
